paper_design_summary: The supplied document is Haase and Hanel's Artificial muses, already catalogued as c156, and is misfiled under the Mir Djawadi and Fahr c493 record (supplied PDF p. 1; c156 journal PDF pp. 1-2). The supplied study analyzed Alternative Uses Test responses from 100 Prolific participants and responses separately generated by five chatbots, followed by a GPT-4 comparison using the same humans; participants were not assigned AI assistance (pp. 4, 7, 11-12). Six human raters and an AUT-trained language model scored originality for the main comparison, only the automated scorer evaluated GPT-4, and counts of ideas measured fluency (pp. 4, 7, 12-13).

studies.label: Alternative Uses Test: human versus chatbot output; GPT-4 follow-up on the same human sample (misfiled Haase and Hanel preprint)

assignment.what_was_assigned: No person was assigned to generative-AI assistance. The between-source comparison is human versus chatbot-generated responses. Human prompt order was randomized; prompt and idea order for raters were also randomized. Repeated prompts do not constitute randomized AI/no-AI conditions.
assignment.quote: In the present study, we compared the creativity of GAI chatbots with humans: We applied the Alternative Uses Test (AUT28) to 100 human participants and five GAI.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 4, Results; p. 12, Materials and Procedure (prompt/rating order only).
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration statement found in the supplied PDF (pp. 1-17).

arms.name: Humans
arms.description: Prolific participants independently supplying AUT responses, three minutes per object; no AI assistance supplied by the study (pp. 11-12, Methodology).

arms.name: GAI chatbots
arms.description: The main originality analysis uses Alpa.ai, Copy.ai, ChatGPT version 3, AI21 Studio, and YouChat, which independently generated AUT responses; these systems are not additional people. Prompt: What can you do with [prompt]?, with up to three follow-ups. Alpa.ai supplied no pants response (pp. 11-12, Methodology; p. 7, Figure 2 note). The exact set of systems underlying the fluency ratio is not specified in the main-text summary (p. 8).

arms.name: GPT-4
arms.description: Added after the main analyses; separately generated AUT responses were scored only by the automated rater and compared with the same human sample (p. 7, GPT-4; p. 12, Procedure).

ai_tool.name_model: Alpa.ai; Copy.ai (freestyle template); ChatGPT version 3 (described in the paper as based on GPT-3); AI21 Studio (Jurassic-1, Playground); YouChat; GPT-4 in follow-up analyses.

Separate chat sessions were used for each object, with What else? up to three times; Copy.ai used more like this three times. Alpa used its maximum-response-length setting (pp. 11-12, Methodology).

task.description: Alternative Uses Test for five objects: pants, ball, tire, fork, and a fifth object inconsistently named toothbrush (p. 4, Results) versus tooth (p. 12, Materials; Tooth in p. 5, Table 1). The exact wording of the fifth prompt cannot be settled from this PDF.
task.duration: Three minutes per object for humans (p. 12, Materials); average total completion time 17 minutes (p. 11, Participants).

outcomes.name: Originality rated by six human raters
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Six human raters, blind to response source, used the Consensual Assessment Technique and a 1-5 originality scale (p. 12, Procedure). Their domain expertise is not stated. Scores were averaged across responses for each creator and prompt (p. 4, Results). Intraclass correlations ranged from .85 to .94; the linear mixed model used random intercepts and slopes for the five prompts, with per-prompt t-tests and counts above the best chatbot as further summaries (p. 4, Originality; p. 5, Table 1). The unit is the creator (participant for humans; system for chatbots), with repeated prompt-level scores. GPT-4 was not human-rated.

outcomes.name: Originality scored by an AUT-trained language model
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: A language model trained on prior human AUT ratings (Organisciak et al., reference 32) scored human and chatbot responses (p. 12, Procedure). Correlation with the mean human rating: rs = .78 - .94, ps < .0001 (p. 4, Originality). Scores were averaged by creator and prompt and analyzed using the second mixed model, per-prompt t-tests, and counts above the best chatbot (pp. 4-5). GPT-4 was scored only by this automated rater (p. 7). No primary/secondary outcome designation is stated.

Tooth: M_H = 2.72, SD_H = 0.36; M_GAI = 2.49, SD_GAI = 0.1; t = 3.99, p = .002, d = 0.65; H > GAI = 65. H > GAI counts humans above the best chatbot. contrasts.reported: Humans more creative than GPT-4: 2 for pants, 29 for ball, none for tire, 3 for fork, and 13 for tooth; on average, 9.4 humans across prompts. These counts are printed in the text. Originality levels are plotted in Figure 3; numerical arm means/SDs and an inferential test for this comparison are not reported. AI-rated only.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 7, GPT-4 (all outperformer counts and automated-only rating); p. 8, Figure 3 (graphical originality levels).

outcomes.name: Fluency (number of ideas)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Sum of ideas from each participant or chatbot, counted by the AI scorer and each of the six human raters; counts varied slightly with exclusion of irrelevant answers (p. 13, Procedure continuation). Rater variants are retained as one outcome. Chatbots could receive up to three follow-up prompts (p. 12, Materials), making the generation conditions unequal. Full comparison statistics are referred to supplemental materials, which are absent from this PDF (p. 8, Fluency).

contrasts.reported: The GAI chatbots came up with 2-3 times more ideas than humans after most were prompted multiple times. Full fluency comparison results are referred to supplemental materials; exact arm means, SDs, and comparison tests are not supplied here. The summary does not specify whether GPT-4 is included in this ratio.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 8, Fluency; p. 13, Procedure continuation (count definition).

eligibility.reason: These final judgments refer to the intended c493 record, Artificial Intelligence and Human Creativity by Mir Djawadi and Fahr, identified in candidates.json as AEARCTR-0016306. The supplied PDF instead identifies Haase and Hanel's Artificial muses on p. 1; retrieval.json links that file to arXiv 2303.12003, and its title, authors, and participant description match the c156 journal PDF (pp. 1-2). No matching c493 source was available for this review, so random assignment of AI assistance, the number of people analyzed, and output-based outcome scoring cannot be confirmed for c493. Unverified candidate notes do not establish any criterion. The retained study fields describe only the misfiled Haase-Hanel paper: it is ai_vs_human context and fails criterion 1 because only prompt/rating order was randomized (PDF pp. 4, 12); it meets criterion 2 with 100 people analyzed (pp. 4, 11), and meets criterion 3 through originality ratings and idea counts on responses (pp. 4, 12-13). Those source-only judgments must not be transferred to the intended c493 study. The availability of a c493 results report or linked paper elsewhere remains unverified.

one_line_finding: The Haase-Hanel PDF misfiled under c493 found no clear overall originality difference between responses from 100 analyzed humans and five chatbots (human-rated B = -0.21, p = .218; AI-rated B = -0.18, p = .241; p. 4), while 9.4 humans on average outscored GPT-4 across prompts (p. 7).
open_questions: The intended Mir Djawadi and Fahr c493 source is missing: obtain the registration/full text for AEARCTR-0016306 before judging that study. The actual supplied paper is already catalogued as c156. Public results/link availability was not verified.
The fifth AUT prompt is toothbrush in Results (p. 4), but tooth in Materials (p. 12) and Table 1 (p. 5); the exact administered prompt is unresolved.
The mixed-model reference group/predictor coding is not reported (p. 4, Originality), so the signed B coefficients cannot be recoded to AI-minus-human effects from this PDF.
The preprint refers to supplemental materials that are not included; full fluency comparison statistics and supplementary reliability/figure details require those materials (pp. 4-5, 8).
notes: Both raw forms parsed successfully. The complete c493 markdown conversion was read, including the reference section through PDF p. 17; there are no appended supplementary pages. All retained numerical findings were checked in PDF text, and all Table 1 cells were checked with PyMuPDF table extraction. No effect sizes were calculated. Primary status is not_stated because the PDF does not designate primary or secondary outcomes; a preferred atlas measure is not a paper-declared primary outcome. ai_available_when_produced = mixed denotes the combination of unaided human creators and AI creators; no human AI-assistance treatment or withdrawal task was studied. The GPT-4 addition is a later model comparison using the same human sample, not an after_ai human outcome. The paper additionally reports: Across all prompts, 32.8 humans were more original than the most original GAI (p. 4, Originality); the sentence does not specify a single scorer, so it is retained here without assigning it to either rating outcome. The aggregate main comparison uses five systems, but Alpa.ai returned no pants response (p. 7, Figure 2 note; p. 12, Materials); chatbot counts are not people counts. No numeric facts about the intended Mir Djawadi and Fahr trial were imported from unverified candidate notes. Pure comparisons among chatbots in Figures 2/S2 and 3 do not establish a human AI-assistance effect. Reconciliation counts substantive differences in recorded facts, classifications, or included results; equivalent wording and information merely relocated within a form are not counted. n_unresolved counts unresolved entries in reconciliation.differences; the shared missing-supplement limitation is recorded separately above. Finalization: no files matching forms/challenges/c493.*.json were present, so challenge_resolution is empty and its action counts are zero. The full supplied markdown was reread through the references, with no appended supplement; recorded numerical findings were rechecked against PDF text and every Table 1 cell against PyMuPDF table extraction. The c156 journal PDF title/authors and participant description were also rechecked on pp. 1-2. Eligibility is changed from judgments about the misfiled PDF to unclear for the intended c493 record on every criterion; context_class is none because no context classification is established for that record. The unrelated study fields remain only as an explicitly identified record of the retrieval error. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as historical provenance and therefore still contains the earlier source-only eligibility judgments. final.open_items covers all open_questions and all three unresolved reconciliation differences, consolidating duplicate issues; n_open counts challenge actions only, not these open items. No web search or external-source retrieval was performed.
